```{r cop-empirical-call, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
  Donor = names(cop_oil_postshock$Y)[-1],
  Weight = as.numeric(out_cop$linear_combinations)
)

knitr::kable(
  weight_df,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "DBW donor weights for the COP empirical application."
)

target_y <- as.numeric(cop_oil_postshock$Y[[1]])
shock_t0 <- cop_oil_postshock$shock_time_vec[1]
pred_day <- shock_t0 + 1

plot_df <- data.frame(
  Day = 1:pred_day,
  COP = target_y[1:pred_day]
)

forecast_points <- data.frame(
  Day = c(pred_day, pred_day - 0.15, pred_day + 0.15, pred_day + 0.30),
  Method = factor(
    c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Arithmetic mean", "DBW adjusted"),
    levels = c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Arithmetic mean", "DBW adjusted")
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.numeric(target_y[pred_day]),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$unadjusted),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$arithmetic_mean),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$adjusted)
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = plot_df, aes(x = Day, y = COP), color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = plot_df, aes(x = Day, y = COP), color = "black") +
  geom_point(
    data = forecast_points,
    aes(x = Day, y = Value, color = Method, shape = Method),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Actual" = "black",
    "Unadjusted" = "red",
    "Arithmetic mean" = "blue",
    "DBW adjusted" = "darkgreen"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "COP path up to the forecast date with postshock forecast comparison",
    x = "Day in local shock window",
    y = "COP price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## MultiPool extension

### Motivation

The single-pool donor adjustment treats all historical donor episodes as belonging to a common donor set. In the COP application, however, this may be restrictive because the March 2020 collapse plausibly reflected multiple channels, including oil-market supply disruptions and broader demand or financial-stress effects. A MultiPool extension allows these channels to be represented separately by grouping donor episodes into economically interpretable pools and aggregating their contributions afterwards.

### Pool definition

Using the same COP shock windows as in the baseline empirical analysis, we partition the donor episodes into two pools. The late-November 2014 episode is assigned to a **supply** pool because it is naturally associated with the OPEC-related oil-price collapse. The March and September 2008 episodes are assigned to a **demand** pool, as they are more closely associated with crisis-driven market stress and demand contraction.

Formally, the pool structure is specified as
\[
\texttt{pools} =
\{\texttt{supply} = (\texttt{Y\_2014\_11\_28}),\;
\texttt{demand} = (\texttt{Y\_2008\_03\_17}, \texttt{Y\_2008\_09\_09}, \texttt{Y\_2008\_09\_15}, \texttt{Y\_2008\_09\_29})\}.
\]

### MultiPool implementation

We apply the MultiPool version of `SynthPrediction()` using the same aligned COP outcome and covariate series as in the baseline case. In this experiment, donor balancing weights are applied within each pool (`pool_use_dbw = TRUE`), while the baseline target forecast is kept as the unweighted ARIMA/ARIMAX component (`base_use_dbw = FALSE`).

We consider two aggregation rules across pools:

1. **Sum aggregation** (`pool_agg = "sum"`), which adds the estimated pool-level shock effects;
2. **Weighted aggregation** (`pool_agg = "weighted"`), which combines the pool-level shock effects using user-specified pool weights.

This comparison allows us to assess whether separating supply-side and demand-side donor pools yields a more interpretable or more accurate postshock adjustment than the single-pool specification.
```{r cop-multipool-call, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
library(knitr)

pre_len  <- 30L
post_len <- 1L
k <- 1L

Y_series_list          <- cop_oil_postshock$Y
covariates_series_list <- cop_oil_postshock$X

shock_time_vec   <- rep(pre_len,  length(Y_series_list))
shock_length_vec <- rep(post_len, length(Y_series_list))

pools <- list(
  supply = c("Y_2014_11_28"),
  demand = c("Y_2008_03_17", "Y_2008_09_09", "Y_2008_09_15", "Y_2008_09_29")
)

# MultiPool with additive aggregation
out_sum <- SynthPrediction(
  Y_series_list          = Y_series_list,
  covariates_series_list = covariates_series_list,
  shock_time_vec         = shock_time_vec,
  shock_length_vec       = shock_length_vec,
  k                      = k,
  pools                  = pools,
  pool_agg               = "sum",
  base_use_dbw           = FALSE,
  pool_use_dbw           = TRUE,
  plots                  = FALSE
)

# MultiPool with weighted aggregation
out_wsum <- SynthPrediction(
  Y_series_list          = Y_series_list,
  covariates_series_list = covariates_series_list,
  shock_time_vec         = shock_time_vec,
  shock_length_vec       = shock_length_vec,
  k                      = k,
  pools                  = pools,
  pool_agg               = "weighted",
  pool_weights           = c(supply = 0.9, demand = 0.9),
  base_use_dbw           = FALSE,
  pool_use_dbw           = TRUE,
  plots                  = FALSE
)

multipool_df <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Single-pool DBW", "MultiPool (sum)", "MultiPool (weighted)"),
  Value  = c(
    as.numeric(cop_oil_postshock$Y[[1]][pre_len + 1]),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$unadjusted),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$adjusted),
    as.numeric(out_sum$predictions$adjusted_multipool),
    as.numeric(out_wsum$predictions$adjusted_multipool)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  multipool_df,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Forecast comparison for the COP empirical application under MultiPool specifications."
)
target_y <- as.numeric(cop_oil_postshock$Y[[1]])
pred_day <- pre_len + 1L

path_df <- data.frame(
  Day = seq_len(pred_day),
  Price = target_y[seq_len(pred_day)]
)

forecast_df <- data.frame(
  Day = c(pred_day, pred_day + 0.10, pred_day + 0.20, pred_day + 0.30, pred_day + 0.40),
  Method = factor(
    c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Single-pool DBW", "MultiPool (sum)", "MultiPool (weighted)"),
    levels = c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Single-pool DBW", "MultiPool (sum)", "MultiPool (weighted)")
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.numeric(cop_oil_postshock$Y[[1]][pred_day]),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$unadjusted),
    as.numeric(out_cop$predictions$adjusted),
    as.numeric(out_sum$predictions$adjusted_multipool),
    as.numeric(out_wsum$predictions$adjusted_multipool)
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = path_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Price),
    color = "grey55",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = path_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Price),
    color = "black",
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Value, color = Method, shape = Method),
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Actual" = "black",
    "Unadjusted" = "#F4A3A3",
    "Single-pool DBW" = "#8DB6F2",
    "MultiPool (sum)" = "#9ED9A3",
    "MultiPool (weighted)" = "#C8A2E8"
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Actual" = 16,
    "Unadjusted" = 17,
    "Single-pool DBW" = 15,
    "MultiPool (sum)" = 18,
    "MultiPool (weighted)" = 3
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "COP path up to the forecast date under single-pool and MultiPool specifications",
    x = "Day in local shock window",
    y = "COP price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Summary and discussion

In this empirical section we applied the postshock forecasting framework to the ConocoPhillips data set using the processed package object `cop_oil_postshock`. The COVID-19 oil-price collapse of 9 March 2020 was treated as the target episode, while five earlier crisis windows from 2008 and 2014 served as donor episodes. The packaged object contains the aligned target and donor outcome series, the corresponding macro-financial covariate matrices, and the associated shock metadata, allowing the empirical workflow to be reproduced directly through the package interface.

The baseline empirical results illustrate the contribution of donor information relative to the unadjusted ARIMAX forecast. The unadjusted forecast, obtained by extrapolating the pre-shock target dynamics without any donor-based correction, lies substantially above the realised COP price on the shock date. Both the arithmetic-mean adjustment and the DBW-adjusted forecast move closer to the realised value, with the DBW-adjusted version performing slightly better in this case. This supports the idea that reweighting donor episodes according to pre-shock similarity can improve postshock prediction relative to simple averaging.

The MultiPool extension further enriches the empirical analysis by allowing donor episodes to be partitioned into economically interpretable groups. In the COP application, the donor episodes were separated into supply-related and demand-related pools, reflecting the view that the March 2020 collapse likely combined multiple transmission channels. The MultiPool results show that this extension can provide a more structured and interpretable decomposition of the postshock adjustment, while also yielding forecasts that are competitive with, and in this case slightly closer to the realised value than, the single-pool DBW forecast.

Overall, the COP case study demonstrates that the proposed framework can transfer information from historical shock episodes to a new target event in a reproducible and modular way. The same package workflow can be adapted to alternative donor structures, additional pooling rules, or other financial and macroeconomic time series, making the framework flexible for a broad class of postshock forecasting problems.

# Empirical Application: IYG Volatility around the 2016 U.S. Election

## Empirical setting and evaluation target

This section illustrates the use of `SynthVolForecast()` on a real-data volatility forecasting problem. The target episode is the 2016 U.S. election, and the target asset is IYG, a financial-sector ETF. The goal is to evaluate whether donor post-shock volatility behavior from related historical events can improve a one-step-ahead post-shock variance forecast.

Because the latent conditional variance is not directly observed in real financial data, evaluation is based on the next-day squared return of the target series. The forecasts reported below are variance forecasts, while the visualization uses a square-root volatility-proxy scale for readability.

## Candidate donor pools

The experiment uses the package data object `iyg_onestep_input`, which contains three ready-to-use donor-pool specifications: `all`, `restricted`, and `elections_only`.

```{r iyg-load-data, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

data("iyg_onestep_input")

names(iyg_onestep_input$inputs)

```

We compare three analyst-specified donor-pool choices. The `all` pool includes all candidate donor episodes and serves as a broad benchmark. The `restricted` pool keeps the 2012 Election, Brexit Poll Released, and Brexit episodes, which are intended to be more comparable political-uncertainty shocks. The `elections_only` pool uses only previous U.S. presidential elections, providing a same-event-type benchmark.

```{r iyg-donor-pools-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

iyg_pool_table <- data.frame(

  Donor_Pool = c("All donors", "Restricted", "Elections only"),

  Donor_Episodes = c(

    paste(iyg_onestep_input$inputs$all$donor_events, collapse = ", "),

    paste(iyg_onestep_input$inputs$restricted$donor_events, collapse = ", "),

    paste(iyg_onestep_input$inputs$elections_only$donor_events, collapse = ", ")

  ),

  check.names = FALSE

)

knitr::kable(

  iyg_pool_table,

  caption = "Donor-pool specifications for the IYG volatility application."

)

```

The donor-pool definitions are treated as analyst-specified inputs rather than being selected ex post based on forecast accuracy. This design allows the application to evaluate how different substantive choices about donor comparability affect the resulting volatility adjustment.

## Package workflow

For each donor-pool specification, the packaged object provides the complete input required by `SynthVolForecast()`: the target and donor return series, the donor covariate series, the target covariates used for DBW matching, and the aligned shock-time metadata. The same function call is then applied to each donor pool.

```{r iyg-run-restricted, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

iyg_restricted <- iyg_onestep_input$inputs$restricted

svf_out_restricted <- SynthVolForecast(

  Y_series_list = iyg_restricted$Y_series_list,

  covariates_series_list = iyg_restricted$covariates_series_list,

  target_covariates = iyg_restricted$target_covariates,

  shock_time_vec = iyg_restricted$shock_time_vec,

  shock_length_vec = iyg_restricted$shock_length_vec,

  k = 1,

  dbw_indices = 1:ncol(iyg_restricted$target_covariates),

  covariate_indices = NULL,

  plots = FALSE,

  return_fits = TRUE,

  max.p = 3,

  max.q = 3,

  vcov.type = "robust"

)

```

```{r iyg-run-all-and-elections, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

iyg_all <- iyg_onestep_input$inputs$all

svf_out_all <- SynthVolForecast(

  Y_series_list = iyg_all$Y_series_list,

  covariates_series_list = iyg_all$covariates_series_list,

  target_covariates = iyg_all$target_covariates,

  shock_time_vec = iyg_all$shock_time_vec,

  shock_length_vec = iyg_all$shock_length_vec,

  k = 1,

  dbw_indices = 1:ncol(iyg_all$target_covariates),

  covariate_indices = NULL,

  plots = FALSE,

  return_fits = TRUE,

  max.p = 3,

  max.q = 3,

  vcov.type = "robust"

)

iyg_elections <- iyg_onestep_input$inputs$elections_only

svf_out_elec <- SynthVolForecast(

  Y_series_list = iyg_elections$Y_series_list,

  covariates_series_list = iyg_elections$covariates_series_list,

  target_covariates = iyg_elections$target_covariates,

  shock_time_vec = iyg_elections$shock_time_vec,

  shock_length_vec = iyg_elections$shock_length_vec,

  k = 1,

  dbw_indices = 1:ncol(iyg_elections$target_covariates),

  covariate_indices = NULL,

  plots = FALSE,

  return_fits = TRUE,

  max.p = 3,

  max.q = 3,

  vcov.type = "robust"

)

```

## Forecast comparison across donor-pool specifications

The observed next-day squared return is used as the realized-variance proxy for

evaluating the one-step-ahead variance forecast.

```{r iyg-results-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

target_reaction_proxy <- as.numeric(

  iyg_restricted$Y_series_list[[1]][

    iyg_onestep_input$evaluation$proxy_index

  ]^2

)

iyg_results <- data.frame(

  Specification = c("Restricted", "Elections only", "All donors"),

  Unadjusted = c(

    as.numeric(svf_out_restricted$predictions$unadjusted),

    as.numeric(svf_out_elec$predictions$unadjusted),

    as.numeric(svf_out_all$predictions$unadjusted)

  ),

  `DBW adjusted` = c(

    as.numeric(svf_out_restricted$predictions$adjusted),

    as.numeric(svf_out_elec$predictions$adjusted),

    as.numeric(svf_out_all$predictions$adjusted)

  ),

  `Arithmetic mean` = c(

    as.numeric(svf_out_restricted$predictions$arithmetic_mean),

    as.numeric(svf_out_elec$predictions$arithmetic_mean),

    as.numeric(svf_out_all$predictions$arithmetic_mean)

  ),

  check.names = FALSE

)

iyg_results$`Observed proxy` <- target_reaction_proxy

iyg_results$`AE DBW` <- abs(iyg_results$`DBW adjusted` - target_reaction_proxy)

iyg_results$`AE arithmetic` <- abs(iyg_results$`Arithmetic mean` - target_reaction_proxy)

knitr::kable(

  iyg_results,

  digits = 6,

  caption = "One-step post-shock variance forecasts for IYG under alternative donor-pool specifications."

)

```

The unadjusted GARCH forecast is much smaller than the realized-variance proxy, suggesting that the pre-shock target volatility model alone does not fully capture the post-shock volatility response. Donor-based adjustment substantially raises the one-step variance forecast. Among the three donor-pool specifications, the restricted pool produces the closest DBW-adjusted forecast to the realized variance proxy. The elections-only pool under-adjusts, while the full donor pool improves relative to the raw forecast but is less accurate than the restricted pool.

The table reports forecasts on the variance scale. The following figure plots the same forecast-day comparison on a square-root volatility-proxy scale, together with the local absolute-return path of the target episode.

```{r iyg-volatility-comparison-plot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}

target_y <- as.numeric(iyg_restricted$Y_series_list[[1]])

shock_idx <- iyg_restricted$shock_time_vec[1]

forecast_idx <- shock_idx + 1L

hist_idx <- (forecast_idx - 30L):forecast_idx

hist_df <- data.frame(

  day = seq_along(hist_idx),

  value = abs(target_y[hist_idx])

)

compare_df <- data.frame(

  day = c(31, 31.08, 31.16, 31.24, 31.32),

  value = c(

    abs(target_y[forecast_idx]),

    sqrt(as.numeric(svf_out_restricted$predictions$unadjusted)),

    sqrt(as.numeric(svf_out_restricted$predictions$adjusted)),

    sqrt(as.numeric(svf_out_elec$predictions$adjusted)),

    sqrt(as.numeric(svf_out_all$predictions$adjusted))

  ),

  type = factor(

    c(

      "Observed",

      "Unadjusted",

      "Adjusted (restricted)",

      "Adjusted (elections only)",

      "Adjusted (all donors)"

    ),

    levels = c(

      "Observed",

      "Unadjusted",

      "Adjusted (restricted)",

      "Adjusted (elections only)",

      "Adjusted (all donors)"

    )

  )

)

ggplot() +

  geom_line(

    data = hist_df,

    aes(x = day, y = value),

    color = "black",

    linewidth = 0.5

  ) +

  geom_point(

    data = hist_df,

    aes(x = day, y = value),

    color = "black",

    size = 2

  ) +

  geom_point(

    data = compare_df,

    aes(x = day, y = value, color = type, shape = type),

    size = 3.5

  ) +

  scale_color_manual(values = c(

    "Observed" = "black",

    "Unadjusted" = "mediumpurple",

    "Adjusted (restricted)" = "tomato",

    "Adjusted (elections only)" = "steelblue4",

    "Adjusted (all donors)" = "firebrick4"

  )) +

  scale_shape_manual(values = c(

    "Observed" = 16,

    "Unadjusted" = 18,

    "Adjusted (restricted)" = 16,

    "Adjusted (elections only)" = 17,

    "Adjusted (all donors)" = 15

  )) +

  scale_x_continuous(

    breaks = c(1, 10, 20, 30, 31),

    labels = c("1", "10", "20", "30", "Forecast"),

    limits = c(1, 31.45)

  ) +

  labs(

    title = "IYG local volatility trend and forecast-day comparison",

    x = "Day in local shock window",

    y = "Volatility proxy scale",

    color = NULL,

    shape = NULL

  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +

  theme(

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

    legend.position = "right"

  )

```

## Discussion

Taken together, the IYG results suggest that donor-pool composition matters primarily through the magnitude of the implied post-shock volatility uplift. All three donor-pool specifications produce adjusted forecasts above the unadjusted GARCH baseline, indicating that donor information consistently contributes a positive short-horizon volatility correction.

At the same time, the results show that a broader donor pool is not automatically preferable. The full donor pool includes more historical episodes, but this can dilute the adjustment when less comparable episodes receive positive weight. The elections-only pool is transparent from an event-type perspective, but it does not generate a sufficiently large volatility adjustment in this case. The restricted pool balances event comparability and broader political-uncertainty relevance, and it produces the closest DBW-adjusted forecast to the realized variance proxy.

This application complements the simulation study by showing that the same donor-based variance-adjustment logic can be applied to a real financial volatility setting using the packaged `iyg_onestep_input` object. It also illustrates that the software is useful not only for producing forecasts after a donor pool has been specified, but also for comparing how different substantive
donor-pool choices affect the resulting post-shock volatility adjustment.

# Empirical Extension: Apple in the Presence of Control Shocks

The Apple example is presented here as a modular validation exercise for the package. In particular, it illustrates that when the target window is short and a fully automatic time-series baseline is less appealing, the package can still be used effectively for donor-side shock-effect estimation, donor balancing weights (DBW), and control-shock regressor construction. Rather than relying on a single end-to-end automatic forecasting routine, this experiment combines a user-specified target-side baseline with the package’s donor-side adjustment machinery.

## Motivation and empirical setting

Apple provides a useful case study because product-release events often generate stock-price movements that may be confounded by broader market forces. In such settings, the observed postshock movement in the target series need not be attributable solely to the event of interest. Instead, it may reflect both an event-specific component and a more general background movement. This motivates a control-shock formulation, in which the forecasting procedure attempts to isolate the event-related adjustment while explicitly controlling for an additional non-target shock.

Following the general validation logic of the Apple case study, we treat one Apple event window as the target episode and use several earlier Apple-related windows as donor episodes. The donor windows are chosen to reflect similar event environments while still allowing heterogeneity in the realized postshock responses. As in the ConocoPhillips application, the windows are locally aligned and the variables are inflation-adjusted before analysis.

## Empirical implementation using the packaged data object

To keep the experiment reproducible, we use the packaged object aapl_onestep_input. This object stores the processed target and donor inputs required for the one-step Apple control-shock experiment. In particular, it contains the aligned target and donor outcome series, the donor-weighting covariate series, the local shock-timing information, the target baseline window, and the key dates needed for the control-shock specification.

This empirical extension should not be viewed as an exact reproduction of the original Apple experiment. Instead, it is designed to show how the package can still be used when the target-side baseline is replaced by a simpler and more natural local regression. In the present setup, the donor-side shock effects and DBW weights are obtained from the package machinery, while the target-side forecast is produced by a one-step regression model using the observed values on 2020-11-10 to predict the Apple closing price on 2020-11-11.

More specifically, the target-side baseline is a one-step local regression of the next-day Apple closing price on the current Apple closing price, the contemporaneous S&P 500 level, the contemporaneous 13-week Treasury bill rate, and a control-shock dummy. The control-shock regressor is constructed using the package helper build_control_xreg(), so the control-shock extension remains fully integrated with the package’s data-handling conventions even though the target-side baseline is user-specified rather than fully automatic.

On the donor side, the package is used to estimate donor shock effects and to compute DBW weights. These donor effects are then aggregated into a weighted adjustment and added to the baseline forecast. We also report a simple mean-adjustment benchmark based on the unweighted average donor effect. This allows us to compare the contribution of the donor-weighting step to the final forecast improvement.
```{r,echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
if (!exists("aapl_onestep_input")) {
  load("../../data/aapl_onestep_input.rda")
}

Y_series_list     <- aapl_onestep_input$Y_series_list
X_for_dbw         <- aapl_onestep_input$X_for_dbw
shock_time_vec    <- aapl_onestep_input$shock_time_vec
shock_length_vec  <- aapl_onestep_input$shock_length_vec
Z_tgt_base        <- aapl_onestep_input$Z_tgt_base
control_shock_day <- aapl_onestep_input$control_shock_day
target_day        <- aapl_onestep_input$target_day

out_pkg <- SynthPrediction(
  Y_series_list = Y_series_list,
  covariates_series_list = X_for_dbw,
  shock_time_vec = shock_time_vec,
  shock_length_vec = shock_length_vec,
  k = 1,
  use_dbw = TRUE,
  dbw_indices = 1:2,
  covariate_indices = NULL,
  arima_order = NULL,
  seasonal = FALSE,
  control_shocks = NULL,
  dbw_center = TRUE,
  dbw_scale = TRUE,
  days_before_shocktime_vec = 10L,
  plots = FALSE
)

omega_vec      <- as.numeric(out_pkg$meta$omega_vec)
omega_combined <- as.numeric(out_pkg$meta$combined_omega)

n_base <- nrow(Z_tgt_base)

train_dat <- data.frame(
  Y    = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[2:n_base, "AAPL"]),
  lagY = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[1:(n_base - 1), "AAPL"]),
  GSPC = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[1:(n_base - 1), "GSPC"]),
  IRX  = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[1:(n_base - 1), "IRX"])
)

idx_ctrl <- which(as.Date(index(Z_tgt_base))[1:(n_base - 1)] == control_shock_day)

C_train <- build_control_xreg(
  last = nrow(train_dat),
  control_spec = list(
    list(time = as.integer(idx_ctrl), length = 1L, shape = "point")
  )
)

train_dat <- cbind(train_dat, as.data.frame(C_train))

fit_base <- lm(Y ~ lagY + GSPC + IRX + ctrl_shock_1, data = train_dat)

newdata_1110 <- data.frame(
  lagY = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[n_base, "AAPL"]),
  GSPC = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[n_base, "GSPC"]),
  IRX  = as.numeric(Z_tgt_base[n_base, "IRX"]),
  ctrl_shock_1 = 0
)

yhat_base  <- as.numeric(predict(fit_base, newdata = newdata_1110))
yhat_dbw   <- yhat_base + omega_combined
yhat_equal <- yhat_base + mean(omega_vec)
y_true     <- as.numeric(Y_series_list[[1]][shock_time_vec[1]])
cat("yhat_base: ", yhat_base, "\n")
cat("yhat_dbw: ", yhat_dbw, "\n")
cat("yhat_equal: ", yhat_equal, "\n")

```
```{r aapl-onestep-plot, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)

aapl_target_y <- as.numeric(Y_series_list[[1]])
aapl_n <- length(aapl_target_y)

plot_df <- data.frame(
  Day = seq_len(aapl_n),
  Price = aapl_target_y
)

forecast_df <- data.frame(
  Day = c(shock_time_vec[1], shock_time_vec[1] + 0.18, shock_time_vec[1] + 0.36),
  Value = c(y_true, yhat_base, yhat_dbw),
  Label = c("Truth", "Baseline", "Baseline + DBW"),
  x_text = c(shock_time_vec[1] + 0.9, shock_time_vec[1] + 0.9, shock_time_vec[1] + 0.9),
  y_text = c(y_true + 0.45, yhat_base - 0.35, yhat_dbw + 0.85)
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(Day, Price)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(
    data = forecast_df[forecast_df$Label == "Truth", ],
    aes(Day, Value),
    color = "black",
    shape = 16,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = forecast_df[forecast_df$Label == "Baseline", ],
    aes(Day, Value),
    color = "#e78ac3",
    shape = 16,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = forecast_df[forecast_df$Label == "Baseline + DBW", ],
    aes(Day, Value),
    color = "#1f78b4",
    shape = 17,
    size = 2.6
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Value, xend = x_text - 0.08, yend = y_text),
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = x_text, y = y_text, label = Label),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(aapl_n - 8, aapl_n + 3),
    ylim = c(
      min(c(tail(aapl_target_y, 8), yhat_base, yhat_dbw, y_true)) - 1,
      max(c(tail(aapl_target_y, 8), yhat_base, yhat_dbw, y_true)) + 1.4
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Apple one-step forecast near the target date",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Closing stock price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

## Results
The Apple control-shock example shows that the package remains useful even when the target-side baseline is replaced by a simpler one-step local regression. In this experiment, the one-step baseline forecast for Apple on 2020-11-11 is 119.023, while the DBW-adjusted forecast is 119.481 and the mean-adjustment benchmark is 119.721. The realized closing price is 119.490.

The baseline forecast therefore underpredicts the target value, whereas the donor-side adjustment substantially improves accuracy. In particular, the DBW-adjusted forecast is nearly identical to the realized value, with only a very small residual error. The mean-adjustment benchmark also improves on the raw baseline, but it is less accurate than the DBW-based adjustment.

This result is important because the Apple example is not used here as an exact replication of the original paper’s implementation. Instead, it serves as a modular validation exercise. The target-side baseline is replaced by a more natural one-step regression, while the package continues to provide donor-side shock effects, DBW weighting, and control-shock regressors. The strong performance of the adjusted forecast suggests that the donor-side adjustment machinery remains effective even when the automatic target-side baseline is not used.

### Forecast Comparison Under the Original Package-Based Apple Control-Shock Specification
```{r aapl-controlshock-call, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)

data("aapl_control_input")

Y_series_list          <- aapl_control_input$Y
covariates_series_list <- aapl_control_input$X
shock_time_vec         <- aapl_control_input$shock_time_vec
shock_length_vec       <- aapl_control_input$shock_length_vec

# control shock specification for the target window
# replace this with the exact local index you want to use
control_shocks <- list(
  list(time = 10L, length = 1L, shape = "point")
)

out_aapl <- SynthPrediction(
  Y_series_list            = Y_series_list,
  covariates_series_list   = covariates_series_list,
  shock_time_vec           = shock_time_vec,
  shock_length_vec         = shock_length_vec,
  k                        = 1,
  use_dbw                  = TRUE,
  dbw_indices              = 1:2,
  covariate_indices        = NULL,
  seasonal                 = FALSE,
  control_shocks           = control_shocks,
  dbw_center               = TRUE,
  dbw_scale                = TRUE,
  days_before_shocktime_vec = 10L,
  plots                    = FALSE
)

actual_aapl <- as.numeric(
  Y_series_list[[1]][shock_time_vec[1] + 1]
)

aapl_result_df <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Actual", "Unadjusted", "Adjusted"),
  Value  = c(
    actual_aapl,
    as.numeric(out_aapl$predictions$unadjusted),
    as.numeric(out_aapl$predictions$adjusted)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  aapl_result_df,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Forecast comparison for the Apple control-shock experiment."
)

```

 
```{r aapl-plot-data, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
# target path
aapl_target_y <- as.numeric(Y_series_list[[1]])
aapl_n <- length(aapl_target_y)

# actual value at the forecast horizon
actual_aapl <- as.numeric(
  Y_series_list[[1]][shock_time_vec[1] + 1]
)

# predictions
aapl_unadjusted <- as.numeric(out_aapl$predictions$unadjusted)
aapl_adjusted   <- as.numeric(out_aapl$predictions$adjusted)

# main path data
aapl_path_df <- data.frame(
  Day = seq_len(aapl_n),
  Price = aapl_target_y
)

# forecast points at the horizon
aapl_forecast_df <- data.frame(
  Day = c(
    shock_time_vec[1] + 1,
    shock_time_vec[1] + 1.10,
    shock_time_vec[1] + 1.20
  ),
  Method = factor(
    c("True value", "Unadjusted", "Adjusted"),
    levels = c("True value", "Unadjusted", "Adjusted")
  ),
  Value = c(
    actual_aapl,
    aapl_unadjusted,
    aapl_adjusted
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = aapl_path_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Price),
    color = "#e78ac3",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = aapl_path_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Price),
    color = "black",
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = aapl_forecast_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Value, color = Method, shape = Method),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "True value" = "black",
    "Unadjusted" = "#e78ac3",
    "Adjusted" = "#1f78b4"
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "True value" = 16,
    "Unadjusted" = 16,
    "Adjusted" = 3
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Apple target window with postshock forecast comparison",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Closing stock price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The original fully automatic package-based Apple control-shock experiment is no longer used as the main empirical specification here. Instead, it is treated as a benchmark, while the main text focuses on the modular one-step implementation based on aapl_onestep_input.


# Conclusion

This technical report developed a modular postshock forecasting framework for time series with structural breaks in both mean and volatility. The framework combines donor-based adjustment, synthetic weighting, and flexible extensions for more complex empirical settings.

The simulation studies show that donor-based adjustment improves postshock forecasting relative to unadjusted benchmarks, and that the DBW mechanism is especially useful when donor episodes differ in their pre-shock covariate environments. In the volatility setting, the framework also extends naturally to postshock variance prediction through GARCHX-type modeling.

The IYG volatility application further shows that the same donor-based adjustment logic can be used for real-data variance forecasting. In that example, the restricted donor pool produces the closest one-step variance forecast to the realized variance proxy, highlighting that donor-pool composition matters for volatility adjustment.

The empirical case studies highlight two complementary forms of flexibility. In the ConocoPhillips application, the framework improves upon the unadjusted benchmark and can be further enriched through the MultiPool extension, which groups donor episodes into economically interpretable channels. In the Apple example, the control-shock formulation shows that the same forecasting core can also be applied when the observed postshock response is interpreted in the presence of an additional background component.

Taken together, these results show that the package is not limited to a single fixed application template. Instead, it supports a reproducible and modular workflow that can be adapted to alternative donor structures, different economic mechanisms, and richer interpretations of postshock behavior. Possible future work includes broader real-data volatility applications, additional pooling schemes, and further extensions of the control-shock framework.
